cells.tense: Here, with the pen, you are holding a heavy thing without forcing it to move faster than it should.
cells.act: say what you see in them only if they ask
cells.ask: Someone close to you is in the middle of something heavy. Stay with them while it lasts — no fixing, no advice, no stacking it against your own. If they ask your read on what's going on with them, answer that, and stop there.
cells.core:
You can hold a heavy thing without squeezing it. There is a way you stay with something while it gets carried through to the end, and you don't push it faster, don't drop it early, don't make it carry you. The end shows up because you held the middle. Then it goes, and your hands are empty.

The next piece of weight someone brings you, stay with it a while. Not to fix, not to advise, not to stack it against your own. Let their load sit next to yours and keep both whole. You'll feel what it is to be reached by what they carry without getting swallowed by it. That's your own grip turned outward, and it makes the next ending cost less.
cells.sheetLine: You hold it steady while it runs its course.
cells.verb: to bear what must be borne and let it finish
cells.place: where what has been carried through is set down and opened, not sealed

cells.tense: You will be bracing for a future load that hasn't arrived when the next one is simply handed to you.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: One share between you and someone else has drifted out of true. Not the whole history — the next errand, the next hour, the next handover. Make it match what's actually there, say it's settled, then stop counting.
cells.core:
You are already leaning into the next weight before this one sets down. Strength that used to wait on the load has started reaching for it. You grip harder and earlier than the thing earns, and anyone standing near you feels a hand that won't move when they push on it. It isn't hardness yet. It's your strength getting a step beyond the actual bearing.

Look at one small share between you and another person, put it in proportion once, then stop. Fairness is short. If it keeps wanting to become an argument, it isn't fairness you're doing, it's a grip wearing a fairness coat. Adjust the next handover, name it done, and leave the book where it lies. The load stays the size the load is.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping for a weight that hasn't landed yet.
cells.verb: to bear what must be borne and let it finish

cells.tense: Holding anything that heavy felt unsafe once, so the grip you have now is small and goes quiet under a real load.
cells.act: let go of the thing you are gripping
cells.ask: Something small you no longer need — an old mug, a box of papers, a shirt you don't wear. Pick it up, look at it once, set it somewhere it no longer belongs to you, and keep your hands open for a while.
cells.core:
The place where heavy things get carried through feels like somewhere you left. Under a real load, the answer that comes is to withdraw, not to brace, and you're back at the door of somewhere you've already walked out of. Nothing here asks you to hold heavier. Start at the easy end.

Let go of a small thing — an item you already don't need. Hold it once, look at it, set it somewhere it no longer belongs to you, and keep your hands open a while. Empty hands say: release is not the same as failure. When a bigger completion is asked for later, your body will have that small memory to lean on, and the load is easier to carry through the last stretch because you no longer think every release is a loss.
cells.sheetLine: 'Bearing it' feels too much like the door you left.
cells.verb: to bear what must be borne and let it finish
cells.place: where what has been carried through is set down and opened, not sealed

cells.tense: With the pen down, you keep thanking the load for getting carried while the one who bore it goes unmentioned.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think of what you've been quietly working toward these months. Name it to yourself, plainly, no dressing on it. Then take the next step of it as if you chose it, because you did.
cells.core:
You hold steady and you give the credit to luck, or the situation, or the plain fact that things needed doing. Something long-burning got carried through to a shape, and your own hand in it is hard to make out. Strength you don't own still works, but it can't be chosen, because nobody chooses what they can't see.

Remember what drew you in the first place. Not the whole life, the part still alive in you that you've been steering by, and have rarely said plainly even to yourself. Face it once, quietly, without needing an audience or a certificate. That is what turns a trait you have into a thing you do on purpose. The next completion lands differently when you know it was you who chose the direction.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it while giving the credit to the load.
cells.verb: to bear what must be borne and let it finish
cells.place: where what has been carried through is set down and opened, not sealed

attempts.check: The strongest unsupported claim is in Balanced: that the person is already finishing things and moving on cleanly, when a balanced Fortitude in the Creation seat only supports 'capacity to hold form under pressure that is available and can let a finished thing leave.' A reader could reasonably say they are holding several uncompleted things right now, not completing them. The Compassion ask does not depend on my read being right: sitting with someone in what they carry and not fixing it teaches something whether they are mid-completion or not. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that implies their completions are already legible; I will say instead that what has been carried through can be opened hands, which stays true at every status on this card.
